questions.question: How do you read input line by line with `bufio.Scanner`?
questions.title: Reading lines with bufio.Scanner
questions.direct_answer: Create a Scanner from an `io.Reader`, call `Scan` in a loop, and read the current token with `Text` or `Bytes`. The default split function is `ScanLines`. When the loop ends, always check `scanner.Err()` because `Scan` returns false for both normal EOF and failures such as an oversized token or an underlying read error.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `Scan` advances; `Text` and `Bytes` expose the current token.
A false `Scan` result can mean EOF or an error.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`bufio.Scanner` is a token-oriented reader. It wraps any `io.Reader` and uses a split function to decide where one token ends. The default is `ScanLines`, so it is a concise fit for ordinary line-by-line configuration, command input, and bounded text records.

The loop contract is `for scanner.Scan()`. Each successful call advances to one token, which can be obtained as a string with `Text` or as bytes with `Bytes`. The byte view may be replaced by the next scan, so data that must survive should be copied.

For example, scanning `"alpha\nbeta\n"` produces two tokens without newline characters. After the second line, the next Scan returns false because the reader reached EOF. `scanner.Err()` then returns nil, distinguishing that normal end from a failed read.

Scanner is easy to use, but its tokens have a maximum size and its API deliberately hides partial reads. For unusually large records, multiple passes, or delimiter handling with more control, I choose `bufio.Reader`. Whichever tool I use, normal EOF and a real error remain separate outcomes.

sections.title: Scanner turns a byte stream into a token stream
sections.content:
An `io.Reader` has no built-in idea of a line. Scanner owns a buffer and repeatedly asks its split function whether enough bytes are available to return a token, request more input, or report a malformed stream.

`ScanLines` recognizes line endings and drops them from the returned token. Other built-in split functions scan words, bytes, or runes, and custom functions can define application records when their maximum size is controlled.

sections.title: The final error check completes the loop contract
sections.content:
Scan cannot return both a Boolean success and a separate error, so false intentionally covers normal completion and failure. `Err` returns the first non-EOF error observed by the Scanner. Omitting that check turns truncated input into apparently complete input.

`Text` allocates a new string containing the token. `Bytes` avoids that conversion but points at scanner-managed storage that later scans may overwrite. Choose from ownership needs rather than assuming the byte form is always faster.

sections.title: One Scanner loop
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Create Scanner from Reader] --> B{Scan returns true?}
  B -- Yes --> C[Use Text or Bytes]
  C --> B
  B -- No --> D{Err is nil?}
  D -- Yes --> E[Normal EOF]
  D -- No --> F[Return read or token error]
```

questions.question: What is Scanner's token-size limit, and when should you change it?
questions.title: Scanner token limits and bufio.Reader
questions.direct_answer: Scanner uses `bufio.MaxScanTokenSize`, 64 KiB, as its default maximum token buffer; the actual accepted token may be slightly smaller because delimiters may also occupy space. Call `Scanner.Buffer` before the first Scan to supply an initial buffer and a justified maximum. Use `bufio.Reader` when records are genuinely unbounded or need incremental handling.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: The default maximum token buffer is `64 * 1024` bytes.
Delimiter space can make the practical maximum slightly smaller.
Set a real application limit rather than an arbitrary huge number.
Use `bufio.Reader` to handle very large records incrementally.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Scanner is designed for convenient, bounded tokens. By default it can buffer up to `bufio.MaxScanTokenSize`, which is 64 KiB. The documentation notes that the actual maximum token may be lower because the buffer can also need room for a newline or another delimiter.

If the input contract permits larger but still bounded records, call `scanner.Buffer(initial, maximum)` before the first call to Scan. The maximum is a safety limit as well as a capability setting; raising it to an uncontrolled value can let hostile input drive excessive memory use.

For example, a service accepting lines up to 128 KiB can give Scanner a modest initial buffer and a 128 KiB maximum. A 70 KiB line then succeeds, while a record beyond the documented limit stops the scan and appears through `scanner.Err()`.

If a logical record may be many megabytes or has no trustworthy bound, `bufio.Reader` is usually the better model. Methods such as `ReadSlice` can return `ErrBufferFull` with a fragment, allowing the program to process or accumulate pieces deliberately instead of demanding one Scanner token in memory.

sections.title: A token limit is part of the input contract
sections.content:
Scanner must hold enough bytes to identify and return one complete token. Its total source may be enormous without causing a problem, but one token larger than the configured maximum stops scanning.

This makes maximum record length a distinct validation rule. A larger Buffer setting is correct only when the application truly accepts that record size and has a memory budget for concurrent scanners.

sections.title: Concept guide · Scanner token limits and bufio.Reader
sections.content:
`Scanner.Buffer` sets both an optional initial storage slice and the maximum allocation Scanner may use. Calling it after scanning starts panics because buffer policy must be fixed before the state machine begins.

A Reader exposes lower-level delimiter operations and fragments. That creates more code but lets an application stream a huge record, preserve delimiters, perform sequential reads with different methods, or enforce limits while accumulating. The choice is an API-shape decision, not a workaround to avoid checking Scanner errors.

sections.title: Bounded token or incremental record
sections.content:
| Input shape | Scanner choice | Reader choice |
|---|---|---|
| Ordinary bounded lines | Default Scanner | More control than needed |
| Known maximum above 64 KiB | Buffer before Scan | Also valid |
| Unbounded or huge record | Risky one-token allocation | Process fragments |
| Need delimiter retained | Custom split required | ReadString / ReadBytes |

sections.title: Raise the line limit before scanning

questions.question: How does `bufio.Writer` work, and why must `Flush` be checked?
questions.title: Buffered writes and Flush
questions.direct_answer: A `bufio.Writer` collects small writes in memory and sends larger batches to its wrapped `io.Writer`, reducing calls to the underlying destination. Data can remain only in that memory buffer until `Flush` is called. Always check Write and Flush errors; closing the wrapped file does not automatically flush a separate buffered writer.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Small application writes can become fewer underlying writes.
`Flush` forwards pending bytes to the wrapped writer.
Flush returns the underlying write error and must be checked.
Closing the wrapped file does not flush the bufio buffer.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`bufio.Writer` adds an in-memory buffer in front of another `io.Writer`. Small calls such as writing many short CSV fields can be combined, so the underlying file, socket, or test writer receives fewer larger Write calls. This can reduce system-call overhead without changing the destination interface.

A successful `WriteString` may mean only that bytes entered the buffer. `Flush` attempts to send all pending bytes to the wrapped writer, and its error is part of the write result. After an underlying error, the buffered writer remembers it and later writes or Flush calls return that failure.

For example, three short writes into a 16-byte buffer can produce zero underlying calls until Flush. After Flush, the destination contains the complete text and the call counter increases. Without Flush, the program could close or return while those bytes never reached the file.

Flush does not close the wrapped destination, and closing an `*os.File` cannot discover a separate bufio buffer. The owner must flush first, then close the file, checking both errors. I use buffering when writes are fragmented; one already-large `io.Copy` pipeline may not benefit from another wrapper.

sections.title: Acceptance into memory is not delivery to the destination
sections.content:
The writer presents the same `Write` contract to its caller while changing when the wrapped writer is invoked. This layer is transparent only if its lifecycle is completed with Flush.

Buffer size affects batching, not total output semantics. Full buffers may flush automatically during later writes, but the final partial buffer still requires an explicit Flush at the application boundary.

sections.title: Track ownership of both layers
sections.content:
Constructing a buffered writer does not transfer responsibility for the wrapped file unless an outer type documents that behaviour. The code that creates both typically owns the order: finish application writes, flush bufio, optionally sync according to durability requirements, then close the file.

`Available` and `Buffered` can expose current capacity, but normal code should not use them to avoid Flush. They help specialised batching decisions; correctness still depends on returning every write and flush failure.

sections.title: Small writes become one destination write
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Write "go"] --> D[bufio memory]
  B[Write " is"] --> D
  C[Write " ready"] --> D
  D -->|Flush| E[wrapped io.Writer]
  E --> F[check error]
```
